So this sub is probably best re-purposed for Voat-based evolution games. Now I think would be a good time to discuss how we move forward with these games. To start off, I don't want it to go rules heavy. That always makes players lose interest and it is hard enough for me to just find time to doodle some evolutions - let alone be a lawyer.

The Cave game was great. Still a bit of activity going on, but it looks like it has settled down. It was a good fun day. I think if we continue with this we should play a game for a week, then switch to a new one. I also think to keep things from getting too messy - I should be the one to create all the games and basically act as Game Manager (GM). Don't worry, I am a kind and forgiving god. So let's discuss the best way to utilize this subverse. These games tend to work better on a 'chan which leaves everything chronological. The up/downvoat system messes this up slightly. I think the next 3 options are the most plausible moving forward.

Option A - Play the game like the last one. One post, edit all creatures in the comments. This way it is all contained in one easy place. Pro - Easy to archive and keep track of. Con - A real clusterfuck sorting through comments to find new evolutions.

Option B - Run one game in multiple threads. Each submission would be a different species and the subverse sticky would give the general game rules. Pro - Easier to keep track of evolution trees/find new creatures to evolve. Con - Lots of different threads, may be hard keep track of what is affecting what.

Option C - Each post is a new creature. Pros - No comment section to sort through. Cons - Voting system really fucks this up, lots of posts everywhere, could end up as an absolute mess.

Option D - You make a suggestion.

Now I'm going to do an annoying thing and ping all the users of the past game in the comment section. Sorry about this. I think moving forward we need to do a continuation of the cave game. Lots of fun had there.

The Soong Sisters; three of China's most influential political figures of the early 20th century. Chongqing. 1942

From left: Mei-ling, Ai-ling and Ching-ling.

The Soong sisters were three Hainanese Chinese women who were, along with their husbands, amongst China's most significant political figures of the early 20th century. They each played a major role in influencing their husbands, who, along with their own positions of power, ultimately changed the course of Chinese history.

Their father was American-educated Methodist minister Charlie Soong, who made a fortune in banking and printing. All three sisters attended Wesleyan College in Macon, Georgia. Their three brothers were all high-ranking officials in the Republic of China government, one of whom was prominent businessman and politician T. V. Soong who was Governor of the Central Bank of China (1928–1934), Minister of Finance (1928–1933), Minister of Foreign Affairs (1942–1945) and founded the China Development Finance Corporation (CDFC) in 1934.

Ai-ling, the eldest sister (1888–1973), was married to the richest man, Minister of Industry (1927-1928) and Minister of Finance (1933–1944) and Governor of the Central Bank of China (1933–1945) H. H. Kung, who, with his brother-in-law, T.V. Soong was highly influential in determining the economic policies of the Kuomintang-led Nationalist government in the 1930s and 1940s.

Ching-ling (1893 – 1981) was the second wife of Sun Yat-sen, one of the leaders of the 1911 revolution that established the Republic of China, and was often referred to as Madame Sun Yat-sen. She was one of the drafters of the 1954 constitution and Vice President of China from 1959-1975.

Mei-ling, (1898 – 2003), the youngest, was a First Lady of the Republic of China, the wife of Generalissimo and President Chiang Kai-shek who served as the leader of the Republic of China between 1928 and 1975. She was a member of the Legislative Yuan (1930- 1932) and Secretary-General of the Chinese Aeronautical Affairs Commission (1936 - 1938). In 1945 she became a member of the Central Executive Committee of the Kuomintang.

Their marriages and alleged motivations have been summarized in the Maoist saying "One loved money, one loved power, one loved her country"; referring to Ai-ling, Mei-ling, and Ching-ling in that order
